title: How can you practise case interview thinking in ten minutes a day?
description: A case asks you to remember an objective, interpret information and speak at the same time. The most useful practice looks like those real tasks.
hook: You can practise case thinking in ten minutes a day with three short drills that copy what a case actually asks of you: recap something you just heard, do maths out loud, and hold a business problem in your head while you plan the next step. A case asks you to keep a goal in mind, take in new information and talk, all at once. These drills train exactly that, and they fit around a working day.
body:
Practise the real task, not a proxy

Brain-training games can be fun, but getting better at a game mostly makes you better at that game. Evidence that it carries over to performance in something as different as a case interview is limited. The most useful practice looks like the real thing: listening, summarising, calculating and deciding what to look at next, out loud.

The ten-minute routine

DrillTimeWhat it trains
Mental recap3 minSumming up under time pressure
Spoken maths4 minCalculating while explaining
Hold the problem3 minKeeping the goal and numbers in mind

1. Mental recap

Play two minutes of a business podcast or interview, pause it, and explain the three most important points in 60 seconds. Start with "Three things were said" and number them. This is the same skill you use to summarise a chart or deliver a recommendation: choosing what matters and saying it in order.

2. Spoken maths

Practise percentages, growth rates, margins, large-number division and break-even. The twist is to say your approach before you calculate, then say what the answer means. For example:

A café sells 1,200 coffees a day at $4.50. Revenue is 1,200 times $4.50, which is $5,400 a day. At a 30% margin that's $1,620 of profit a day, so each extra 100 cups adds $135.

Check the last step: 100 × $4.50 × 30% = $135. Saying the method first lets an interviewer correct you early, and saying the meaning turns a number into an insight.

3. Hold the problem

Read a short business problem once, put it away, then recall the objective, the key figures and two possible causes. Finish with a 30-second plan for how you would investigate. Here is one to try:

A gym chain's revenue rose 5% last year, from $20M to $21M, but profit halved, from $2M to $1M. The CEO wants profit restored within 12 months.

A strong recall goes like this. The goal is to restore profit to $2M within a year. Costs were $20M − $2M = $18M and are now $21M − $1M = $20M, so costs rose by $2M, about 11%, while revenue grew only 5%. Two possible causes: a big jump in fixed costs such as new sites or rent, or variable costs per member rising faster than prices. The first thing to check is which cost lines grew most.

Notice that working out the cost increase was not in the prompt. Holding the numbers lets you spot what the prompt implies, which is what hypothesis-driven thinking looks like in practice.

Two variations to rotate in

  • The one-sentence chart. Look at an unfamiliar chart for 60 seconds, then summarise it in one sentence that includes a "so what". The next day, check whether you remember the relationship and the implication, not just the axes. The chart drill gives you a new chart each time.
  • Redraw a structure. Read one of the core frameworks, close it, and redraw it from memory. Check the gaps.

Keep an error log

Write down every mistake you notice, in three columns: the mistake, its cause and your next practice action. If you keep losing the client's objective after a calculation, the fix is to box it at the top of your page and point back to it after every result. If you calculate correctly in silence but stumble when explaining aloud, move more of your maths practice to spoken problems.

Once a week, test whether the drills are working by running one unfamiliar case with a partner. Better scores in a drill do not guarantee a better case; the case is the real test.

Common mistakes

  • Long, irregular sessions. Ten minutes most days beats two hours on a Sunday. Tick it off and move on.
  • Silent practice. In the interview you will be talking, so practise talking.
  • Stopping at the number. Every calculation should end with what it means for the client.
  • Only doing what you are good at. Spend most of the time on the drill you find hardest.

Try it now

1. Read this once, look away, and say the goal, the key numbers and the first thing you would check: "A bakery chain's sales are flat at $8M. Flour, which was 10% of sales, has risen in price by 20%. The owner wants to keep profit at $800k."

Show the answer

Goal: keep profit at $800k. Flour cost was 10% × $8M = $800k and is now $800k × 1.2 = $960k, so costs are up $160k and profit falls to $640k if nothing changes. $160k is 2% of sales, so a price rise of about 2% would close the gap, if volumes hold. First check: how sensitive customers are to a small price rise, alongside cheaper flour suppliers.

2. Out loud, method first: a retailer has 250 stores, each with $1.2M of yearly sales. What is total revenue, and what is left if 10% of stores close?

Show the answer

"Total is 250 times $1.2M, which is $300M. 10% of stores is 25 stores, losing 25 times $1.2M, so $30M, leaving $270M, assuming the closed stores are average and no sales move to nearby stores."

3. Play two minutes of any business podcast and recap it in 60 seconds, starting "Three things were said".

Show the answer

A good recap names three points in order of importance, each in one sentence, and ends with what you think the speaker's main message was. If you needed more than 60 seconds, cut the detail, not the structure.

Where to practise next

For more spoken maths, use the case maths drill. The interview skills page collects all three routines with links to free tools, and the list of short daily exercises adds voice and calm drills you can pair with these.
